title: Compute Systems: VMs, GKE, Serverless, VMware Engine, and Orchestration
bodyMarkdown:
## Pick the operating model, then the pricing model, then the automation

Compute questions have three layers. First, how much of the stack you want Google to run (VM, Kubernetes, container, function, VMware). Second, how you pay and what capacity assurance you need (on-demand, commitments, Spot, reservations, sole-tenant). Third, how you keep the fleet reproducible and patched (infrastructure as code, VM Manager). The exam rewards the least operationally heavy option that still meets a stated constraint, and it penalizes "managed" answers that violate a hard requirement such as privileged access, existing VMware tooling, or no interruptions.

## The compute spectrum

| Option | You manage | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|
| Compute Engine | Guest OS and everything above | Full OS control, custom kernels, licensed software, GPUs and TPUs, lift-and-shift |
| [Google Cloud VMware Engine](https://cloud.google.com/vmware-engine/docs/overview) | VMware workloads; Google runs the stack | Keep vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX and HCX tooling and skills unchanged |
| GKE Standard | Node pools, scaling, capacity | Privileged Pods, DaemonSets with host access, specific node shapes |
| GKE Autopilot | Workloads only; billed per Pod requests | Production Kubernetes with minimal operations |
| Cloud Run | Container or source only | Stateless HTTP services, jobs, scale to zero |

### VMware Engine versus Migrate to Virtual Machines

These are frequently confused. VMware Engine runs your VMware environment on **dedicated bare-metal nodes** in Google Cloud, with Google handling deployments, upgrades, management plane backups, health and capacity monitoring. Because the VMware stack stays the same, it is the lowest-change lift-and-shift and also suits data-center exit, burst capacity and disaster recovery, with high-speed connectivity to native Google Cloud services.

[Migrate to Virtual Machines](https://cloud.google.com/migrate/virtual-machines/docs/5.0/concepts/overview) is a different tool: it moves VM instances and disks from on-premises vSphere, AWS, Azure or VMware Engine into native Compute Engine VMs or Persistent Disk volumes. That is re-platforming onto Compute Engine, not keeping VMware. Rule: "keep vCenter, vSAN and NSX unchanged" means VMware Engine; "convert to Compute Engine instances" means Migrate to Virtual Machines.

## Pricing and capacity models

| Model | Discount and terms | Interruption | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| On-demand | None | None | Unpredictable or short-lived load |
| [Spot VMs](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot) | Up to 91% off on-demand for many machine types, GPUs, TPUs and Local SSD; price changes daily | Can be preempted at any time; no SLA | Fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch |
| [Committed use discounts](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/committed-use-discounts-overview) | 1 or 3 years; resource-based or spend-based | None | Steady always-on baselines |
| [Reservations](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/reservations-overview) | Billed at on-demand rate while they exist | None | Guaranteed capacity |
| [Sole-tenant nodes](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/nodes/sole-tenant-nodes) | Billed per full node | None | Dedicated hardware for BYOL or compliance |

**Spot VMs** replaced preemptible VMs and have **no maximum runtime**, but they do not auto-restart, do not live migrate, and carry no SLA. On preemption Compute Engine sends a metadata notification and ACPI signal, then best-effort shutdown for up to 30 seconds; the preemption notice period is configurable as 120 seconds or 0 (the default is 0). You choose a termination action, `STOP` (default; the VM stays in your project and its disks still bill) or `DELETE`. Sustained and committed use discounts do not apply, and free-tier credits do not apply. In a **managed instance group** the group recreates preempted instances, and instance flexibility lets it choose machine types with lower preemption rates. Pair Spot with checkpointing so work resumes after interruption.

**Committed use discounts.** Resource-based CUDs commit to vCPUs, memory, GPUs, Local SSD, sole-tenant nodes or licenses in one region and project, with discounts up to 55% for most machine series and up to 70% for memory-optimized, and **cannot be cancelled**. **Compute flexible CUDs** (spend-based) commit to hourly spend across Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud Run in a billing account, with discounts roughly 16 to 17% on one-year terms rising to 38 to 63% on three-year terms depending on series. The key fact: **neither type guarantees capacity**. Only reservations do, and a reservation can be attached to a resource-based commitment so you get both capacity and discount; the reservation must match the commitment's project, region, machine family and resources. Unused reservations still bill until deleted, so set auto-delete for time-boxed events. Shared reservations let consumer projects use an owner project's capacity.

**Sole-tenant nodes** are physical servers dedicated to your project. They exist for per-core BYOL licensing, compliance isolation and some performance scenarios. You create a node template (a regional resource with a node type such as `n2-node-80-640`), then a node group in a zone, then place VMs on it. Host maintenance happens roughly every four to six weeks with default (live migration), affinity-preserving, or custom policies.

**Decision shorthand.** Steady 24/7 baseline and no interruption tolerated: CUD. Interruptible, restartable batch: Spot in a MIG. Need guaranteed capacity at a known time: reservation. Licensing or isolation mandate: sole-tenant.

## GKE: Autopilot versus Standard

The [cluster mode guide](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/choose-cluster-mode) calls Autopilot the **recommended** mode. GKE manages nodes, bin-packing and scaling and applies security best practices by default, and you pay for the resources your **Pods request**. Standard gives you control over node pools and sizing, you pay per node, and you do the capacity planning. Autopilot prevents privileged Pods by default, so workloads that need privileged access or custom node configuration belong on Standard. You can also run Autopilot-managed workloads inside Standard clusters using compute classes.

Networking: [VPC-native clusters](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/alias-ips) (alias IP ranges) are the default for all new clusters. Nodes use the subnet's primary range; Pods use a secondary range, with each node allocated a `/24` (256 addresses) supporting up to 110 Pods per node in Standard and 32 in Autopilot. Services draw from a GKE-managed range, `34.118.224.0/20` by default on newer versions. Sharing one Pod secondary range between clusters lets one cluster starve the others; when ranges run out you can create a new cluster, lower max Pods per node, or add discontiguous multi-Pod CIDR ranges. Plan Pod ranges before cluster creation.

## Cloud Run and serverless networking

[Cloud Run](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) offers **services** (HTTP request handling with autoscaling), **jobs** (run-to-completion tasks), **worker pools** (pull-based background work without automatic scaling) and **instances**; functions deploy onto the same platform. Services scale out rapidly, remove idle instances, and scale to zero unless you set minimum instances. Billing is **request-based** (pay only while handling requests) or **instance-based** (pay for the instance lifetime). Deployment sources are container images, source code, or functions.

To reach private VPC resources, use [Direct VPC egress](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/vpc-direct-vpc) or a Serverless VPC Access connector. Direct VPC places instances on your subnet, avoiding connector instance costs and extra latency. Cloud Run reserves IPs in blocks of 16 (`/28`), so subnets should be `/26` or larger for IPv4, and a service reserves roughly twice its instance count plus a buffer. Egress setting is either private ranges only or all traffic. Connection establishment on startup can take a minute or more, so use HTTP startup probes that test egress.

## Infrastructure orchestration and patching

- **[Infrastructure Manager](https://cloud.google.com/infrastructure-manager/docs/overview)** is a managed service that deploys Terraform configurations. It creates a Cloud Storage bucket for deployment metadata and state, runs `terraform init`, `validate` and `apply` or `destroy` in an ephemeral Cloud Build environment with automatic retries on transient failures, tracks revisions (config, logs, resources, state), and supports preview deployments to see changes before applying.
- **[Config Connector](https://cloud.google.com/config-connector/docs/overview)** is an open-source Kubernetes add-on whose CRDs let you manage Google Cloud resources declaratively; its controllers reconcile asynchronously using the Config Connector service account, so developers need no direct cloud permissions. Config Controller is the managed variant.
- **[VM Manager](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/vm-manager)** has three parts: patch management (on-demand or scheduled, with configurable rollout across zones and compliance reporting), OS inventory, and OS policies for installing or removing packages. It needs the OS Config agent on VMs, supports Windows and Linux, and is a paid service.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Spot VMs for the always-on baseline.** Cheapest per hour, but interruption and no SLA break the requirement; use CUDs.
- **Expecting a CUD to guarantee capacity.** It does not; add a reservation.
- **Buying resource-based CUDs for a shifting estate.** They cannot be cancelled and are tied to region and project; flexible CUDs fit moving workloads.
- **GKE Standard "to be safe".** Autopilot is recommended; choose Standard only for privileged workloads or node-level control.
- **Undersized Pod secondary ranges.** Exhaustion forces a rebuild or range expansion.
- **Using VMware Engine when you want native VMs.** That is Migrate to Virtual Machines.
- **Cloud Run Direct VPC on a tiny subnet.** IPs are reserved in blocks of 16, so the subnet must be `/26` or larger.
- **Hand-patching VMs and clicking infrastructure into existence.** Use VM Manager and Terraform via Infrastructure Manager.

## Exam tips

- **Stateless container, spiky, scale to zero:** Cloud Run. A MIG or GKE Standard needs more operations and does not scale to zero.
- **Hands-off Kubernetes billed per Pod request:** GKE Autopilot. Privileged or node-specific needs: Standard.
- **Unchanged vSphere, vCenter, vSAN, NSX:** VMware Engine. Convert VMs to Compute Engine: Migrate to Virtual Machines.
- **Steady, uninterrupted baseline:** committed use discounts. Interruptible and checkpointed: Spot VMs in a managed instance group.
- **Guaranteed capacity requires a reservation.** CUDs alone give a discount, not capacity.
- **Spot VMs have no SLA and no max runtime.** Up to 91% discount, 30-second best-effort shutdown, MIGs recreate them.
- **Terraform as a managed service means Infrastructure Manager;** Kubernetes-native resource management means Config Connector; OS patching means VM Manager.
- **Serverless reaching private resources:** Direct VPC egress (preferred, no connector) or a Serverless VPC Access connector.
